Making Software: How is data stored?
Data and Compression
/
How is data stored?
4856 words
|
Dan Hollick
How is data stored?
Invariably, it involves trying to trap electrons in increasingly complicated ways.
╌╌╌╌
Computers depend on memory - the
CPU
6
and
GPU
10
are just data processing machines and the worst thing that could happen is a clock cycle wasted waiting for data due to
latency
12
.
But fast memory is expensive and power hungry so we arrange it into a hierarchy - the closer to the processing unit the faster the memory needs to be at the expense of capacity and as we get further away from the processing unit we can increase the capacity at the expense of speed.
The fastest memory outside of the CPU registers is the L1
Cache
4
which is super tiny, in the region of 64 kilobytes, but super fast, with access speeds around 1ns. The L1 Cache stores both instructions and data with direct access to the CPU and therefore needs to run as close to the clock speed of the CPU as possible. They are fed in turn by slightly larger and slower caches that keep them full.
Caches are a type of memory called
Static Random Access Memory (SRAM)
17
, and outside of the caches are banks of much larger
Dynamic Random Access Memory (DRAM)
8
. DRAM has a much higher capacity, in the tens of Gigabytes, but at the expense of speed, around 60ns. The difference is that static memory holds data for as long as there is power supplied to the bank whereas dynamic memory needs to be refreshed constantly to prevent the data being lost.
Outside of the inboard memory of the caches and RAM is the outboard storage, like your hard disk or solid state drives. Again the capacity increases as the speed decreases, and so these drives are massive, in the terabyte range, but really slow compared to inboard storage. The real advantage of outboard storage is that it can hold data without a power supply, allowing data to be stored for years, even decades.
Because each of these memory solutions is making a different tradeoff when it comes to capacity and read/write speed, their underlying technologies are actually quite different.
Static random access memory
SRAM is the fastest memory largely because it's the simplest. Whereas the other memory types we'll talk about later use clever ways to store an electric or magnetic charge, SRAM uses a bunch of simple
transistors
19
to store a single bit.
There are different types, but you can sort of think of a transistor as a switch. There are three terminals, a source, a drain and a gate. The idea is that if you apply a small voltage between the gate and the source, it induces a large current flow between the source and the drain. We can use this as a switch to control whether or not current flows through the transistor.
Out of these switches we can construct
logic gates
13
and the particular logic gate we need to create some memory is an inverter or a NOT gate, which inverts the signal applied to it. If there is a voltage applied to the inverter, it returns 0v and if there is no voltage it returns a voltage. Confusing, I know.
For our
memory cell
14
, we need two inverters, A and B. We connect the output of inverter A to the input of inverter B, and then the output of inverter B into the input of inverter A. This is called cross coupling and creates a stable feedback loop - if inverter A outputs 1 it feeds that into inverter B which inverts it and outputs 0. That is then fed into inverter A which confirms it should keep outputting 1.
This is how we store data - as long as there is power applied to this circuit inverter A will keep outputting 1. This memory cell is isolated from the rest of the memory by two more transistors attached to something called the
word line
20
. These word line transistors control the access to the
bit lines
2
, one running either side. When we open the access transistors, the current flows down the bit lines to be read by the CPU.
We technically only need to send the signal down one bit line but we send both the signal and the inverse to overcome any noise in the system. If the loop holds a 1, the bit line voltage will go up slightly and if it holds a 0 the voltage will drop slightly. At the end of the bit line are some amplifiers to boost the signal that might degrade slightly if the bit lines are very long.
To write to the cell, we open the access transistors and drive the voltage on the two bit lines - we put a high voltage on one side and a low voltage on the other. This overpowers the signal in the feedback loop and flips the inverters. We can control the state of the inverters by selecting which bit lines to drive high and low. We then stop driving the bit lines and the new state is stored in the loop.
This kind of cell is called a 6T cell because it requires six transistors in total but there are other types with four transistors. These cells are arranged into arrays where the columns are connected by the vertical bit lines and the rows are connected by the horizontal word lines.
To access some memory in a row, we work out from the address which word line it falls on and drive up the voltage of
that word line while driving the voltage of the others down. This causes every cell connected to that word line to send
its signal down the bit lines and into the sense amplifiers.
At the bottom, all the bit lines are connected to a column multiplexer which acts as a switchboard that filters out the columns that the CPU is looking for and that data is sent on to the CPU.
It's much easier to manufacture SRAM like this but the consequence is that we waste a lot of power fetching data we don't need. To mitigate this, we can split the caches that use SRAM into smaller banks - a 1024kb cache can be split into 8 smaller 128kb banks to use less power.
SRAM is really fast, with the biggest speed bottleneck coming from the length of the bit and word lines which increases as the capacity increases. This is why the L1 cache, which needs to be as fast as possible, is kept quite small while the higher level caches can increase in size.
Dynamic random access memory
So if transistor based memory like SRAM is so great, why don't we use it for all RAM? Well, we could but computers would cost ten times as much, be twice the size, and use as much power as a commercial oven. Transistor based memory is very fast but it's incredibly space inefficient and expensive to produce.
We need some other type of storage that is a compromise between the speed of SRAM and the capacity of long term storage - enter Dynamic Random Access Memory (DRAM). It's dynamic in the sense that it needs to be constantly refreshed in order to hold its data, whereas SRAM will hold data as long as it has a power supply. Instead of transistors, DRAM uses tiny
capacitors
5
to store an electric charge which we can read as a bit.
Typically each DRAM memory cell consists of a single capacitor connected to a transistor, called a 1T1C cell. A capacitor is a passive electronic component that stores an electrostatic charge - you can think of it like a tiny battery, although they are quite different, that can hold and release a charge very quickly. The transistor acts as a sort of switch that allows us to charge and discharge the capacitor.
There are two lines connected to the transistor, the word line which is connected to the gate, and the bit line which connects to the other side. When we apply a voltage to the word line it opens the transistor and allows electrons to flow along the bit line into the capacitor allowing us to write to cell by either charging or discharging it. We can also read the voltage along the bit line to read the value.
When the word line has no voltage applied, the transistor shuts and the cell is isolated from the rest of the circuit. Because the scale of everything here is so tiny, even when the transistor is closed the charge slowly leaks out of the capacitor and across the transistor. This is why it's called dynamic RAM, because we have to constantly top up the charge that's in capacitor so we don't lose the data stored there.
You might think that we can alter the charge level to store multiple bits in a single cell but because they are so leaky, we can only reliably use each one to store a single bit of data. With DDR5, more or less the latest standard, a capacitor charge level of
1.1v
is read as a
binary
1
1 and
0v
a binary 0, while the maximum charge of the capacitor is about
1.4v
to accommodate for the charge leaking out.
These single 1T1C memory cells are arranged into rows with the word lines running across an entire row, connecting all the cells together. Rows are stacked one after the other, with the bit lines running down each column connecting each cell. The word and bit lines are separated vertically so they never touch.
Remember that when a word line has a voltage applied to it, the transistor attached to it opens and connects the capacitor to the bit line. So that means that every capacitor in a given row is connected to their respective column bit line at the same time allowing us to read or write to it. At any given time, we can only activate a single row to prevent multiple capacitors on the same bit line being connected which would interfere with one another.
These arrays of memory make up a bank that contain many more rows than columns, we might have over 8,000 columns and over 65,000 rows. These banks are arranged together in the chip either side of a memory bus. When we make a request to RAM, we specify a 32-bit address that contains all the information we need to access just 8 of these cells.
The first 5 bits of the address specify the bank that memory is in and the next 16 bits indicate the row in that bank we want to activate by turning on the word line. The last 10 bits of the address specify the columns we are interested in. All the bit lines in a bank are connected at the bottom to something called a column multiplexer which reads the column address and connects just those 8 bit lines to the output. We can use this system to access any row of 8-bits in the bank.
DRAM has three operations, reading, writing and refreshing. When we read data from a bank, we first need to disconnect all the word lines, or rows, and pre-charge all the bit lines, or columns, to around 0.5v. We need to do this because these bit lines are really long and the capacitors don't have enough charge on their own for us to sense their voltage level. After each bit line is at 0.5v, we cut them off and start connecting the correct row.
At the bottom of each bit line, before the column multiplexer, is a sense amplifier which is designed to detect differences in voltage instead of absolute values. When a bit line is connected to a cell that contains
~1.0v
, the bit line voltage goes up to
0.55v
and when it is connected to a cell with
0v
, the bit line voltage goes down to
0.45v
. The sense amplifiers detect this difference in voltage from the pre-charged level and amplify that bit line to either
0v
or
1v
.
So now all the bit lines in our row are amplified, the row is 'open' and the column multiplexer uses the column address to connect the correct 8 columns to the read driver output and on to the CPU.
When we write data to DRAM, we use the same 32-bit address but we also send the 8-bits we want to write to memory to the write driver, which is connected to the column multiplexer. The process is largely the same as reading, with all the bit lines being pre-charged before a row is opened but this time the column multiplexer connects the 8 bit lines to the write driver that has the 8-bits we want to write.
The write driver is more powerful than the sense amplifiers connected to each bit line and so they can override them, changing the voltage in each bit line to
0v
or
1v
regardless of what it was before. This new voltage replaces whatever was stored in those 8 connected capacitor cells, writing the data to that address.
As mentioned earlier, the tiny transistors allow the charge in each cell to slowly leak out over time so we need to periodically refresh each cell. To do this, we close all the rows in a bank and pre-charge the bit lines like before and then open a single row. The sense amplifiers sense the voltage and drive each bit line in the entire row which restores the correct charge in each cell.
We repeat this process for each row in a bank until the entire bank is fully recharged. We need to do this about every 64ms otherwise the charge in each cell would get too low to reliably know if that cell was a 1. The whole process of refreshing a bank takes a few milliseconds and, of course, we can't use the entire bank during this process.
If the CPU needs some data on a bank that is being refreshed, it has to wait for it which is a bit of a disaster. To mitigate this the memory controller will look for gaps to opportunistically refresh a bank when the CPU isn't currently requesting anything from it. It can also do shorter refreshes if necessary - instead of refreshing the whole bank it can refresh a few rows, sneak in a request and carry on the refresh process.
All the steps involved in reading and writing, like pre-charging the lines, opening the rows, and sensing the columns, takes some time to perform. It's much quicker if the data we need is on a row that's already open, so arranging the memory so that related pieces are on the same row is important.
There are typically 32 banks each with their own column multiplexers, drivers and sense amplifiers so that the banks can be used in parallel. This means there are 32 open rows at any given time and we can arrange the memory to take advantage of that, arranging memory so that related pieces are on the same row across multiple banks.
Solid state drives
The leaky capacitors used in DRAM require constant refreshing which, of course, requires a constant power supply but we need a more permanent way to store data such that it can be preserved across power cycles. We also need more capacity than is practical with the capacitor set up, which is expensive because of its intricate circuitry.
Enter the
Solid State Drive (SSD)
18
, which solves these issues but once again at the expense of read and write speed. The fundamental unit at the center of SSDs is a Charge Trap Flash memory cell which is a tiny cell that can trap electrons and we can use the amount of trapped electrons to store data.
⁂
A Charge Trap cell has three main components, the gate, the charge trap and the channel. Each of these components is separated by a
dielectric
7
barrier that prevents the flow of electrons between them but allows electric fields to pass through. If we ignore the charge trap for a second, this looks sort of like a basic transistor where the gate acts like a switch that allows electrons to flow through the channel.
The way this happens is by applying a positive voltage to the gate which emits an electric field and induces current flow in the channel. The voltage needs to be strong enough to overcome the insulation between them, known as the threshold voltage. If there are negatively charged electrons in the charge trap, they repel this electric field meaning that we need a higher voltage to overcome them.
To put it simply, the more electrons in the charge trap the higher the threshold voltage needs to be on the gate to induce current flow in the channel. Because we know how much voltage we are applying to the gate and we can sense how much current is flowing through the channel, we can determine how much charge is trapped in the cell.
In a Single-Level Cell (SLC) we store a single bit per cell, so the amount of charge in the trap indicates either a 1 or a 0. These days, we largely use Triple-Level Cells (TLC) to store 3-bits per cell by having 8 different electron charge levels per trap. But if the charge trap is insulated from the channel, how do we even get electrons in there?
Here's where it gets gnarly. The width of barrier between the channel and the charge trap is very specifically calculated to be just thin enough to allow electrons to 'jump' it but thick enough that they need to be forced to do so, around 8nm thick. If we apply a strong enough positive voltage to the gate it creates a positive electric field that attracts the negatively charged electrons, forcing them to tunnel through the barrier.
This is technically
quantum tunneling
16
in action - the electrons aren't actually a single point in space but rather a cloud of probabilities. The electric field is strong enough that the probabilities of the electron's location are now on the charge trap side, trapping the electrons there. Yes, your phone is using quantum mechanics to store that picture you just took of your cat.
This is also why SSDs have a limited life span - these very thin barriers degrade a little bit every time we force electrons across them, so over time their ability to store electrons in the charge trap degrades. Luckily this is a super high number of operations but it's also why SSDs aren't great for extremely long term storage.
So far, the types of memory we've looked at have been arranged in single layers, but to increase the storage density SSDs arrange charge trap cells in vertical columns which is why they have this cylindrical shape. We call this vertical column of connected cells a string and the entire string shares the same central channel which connects to a bit line at the top.
Each cell in this vertical column has a separate control gate running horizontally and the process of reading a cell means activating the control gate row and listening on the connected bit line. The idea is that only one cell in a given string (column) can be read or written to at a time, similar to the DRAM approach.
Now imagine we have a bunch of these vertical strings connected together. Each string is a column but the cells in each row share the same control gate which runs horizontally across all strings - these cells are called a page. When a control gate is active, each cell in that page is active at the same time, sending current up the channel to each bit line, reading the entire page at once.
This is actually where this technology gets its name,
NAND flash
15
memory, because it resembles the way a NAND transistor gate connects everything in series. This type of memory is technically called a 3D NAND flash, because as we are about to see it's arranged in a 3D structure.
So far we've kept the structure pretty 2D but the arrangement of cells we've been talking about is a single row and we have multiple rows connected by the same bit line and we group these rows together into blocks.
Here's where it gets confusing - we've stepped up a level of abstraction so now our structure has rows, columns and layers. A row is the structure we've been talking about where each column is string and each row is a page. A column is a vertical slice of this structure that groups all the strings connected to the same bit line. A layer is a horizontal slice selecting all the pages on the same level.
When the SSD gets a request for some data, the address will contain a block number and a page number. First it needs to track down the block and figure out which row that page falls into so we can activate the bit line selector for that row. Then it activates the control gates for that specific page, which communicate their threshold voltages via the current flowing in the channel to the bit line, reading the entire page.
So far we've illustrated these pages as quite small but in reality they are about 16 KB wide, meaning there are about ~50,000 cells in a single page. That's a lot of data for a single page read and so SSDs need to have some DRAM on board to act as
buffer
3
memory, which helps speed up subsequent requests.
Another quirk is that, like DRAM, only one block can be active at a time and so we need to spread the data out onto multiple blocks, usually across multiple chips. Imagine we are trying to stream a large video file from the SSD, if it were all stored in sequence on the same block we would be bottlenecked by the read speed.
If we spread the file out over multiple chips we can read the data in parallel and we can also use something called a super page, which uses the exact same physical page to store data across multiple chips, meaning they share the same address. The SSD controller is in charge of all of this memory management as well spreading the load amongst cells to prolong life. Remember that although SSDs can store data for years, they have a read/write limit that makes them prone to degrading over time.
Hard disk drives
It might seem like a disk drive is outdated technology now because of how ubiquitous SSDs have become in the last decade or so, but in reality they are still one of the cheapest and most reliable forms of long term memory storage. Like with a lot of technology of this sort of age, it's scarcely believable that this combination of incredible material science and clever engineering ever made it out of the research lab.
The core of a
hard disk drive (HDD)
11
is the magnetic disk, known as a platter, which stores the data using magnetic orientation. Typically there are multiple platters arranged in a vertical stack with a slight gap between them. These disks spin around a central spindle connected to a motor at the bottom which spins the disk at very precise rpm, usually 7,200 rpm in consumer devices.
These platters are usually about the same thickness as a CD, just over a millimeter, but the magnetic layer on the top and bottom is incredibly thin at around 120nm. The disk is read by a read/write head on either side that is moved around the disk by an actuator arm.
The tolerances here are incredible. The read/write head sits inside a slider which is designed to use the air resistance created by the spinning disks to lift the head around 15nm above the surface of the disk. Because of these tight tolerances, the arm can only be moved over the disks once they are fully up to speed.
The arm is connected to an actuator with a neodymium coil motor that can precisely control the angle of the arm and therefore the position of the read/write head. There are multiple arms, two for each disk, and they are all connected to the same assembly meaning they are all moved in unison, which will be important for the way we allocate data across the different disks.
I can't easily communicate how fine the tolerances are here - the width of a human hair is between 50,000 and 100,000 nanometers so 15 nanometers is absolutely microscopic. At this size a tiny spec of dust would completely obstruct the read/write head and so the whole drive is sealed to prevent anything entering the enclosure.
So how do we store data on these disks? Well, it's covered in a very thin magnetic layer that is divided into hundreds of thousands of concentric circles around the surface called tracks. Each track is divided into sectors that have a specific structure, with the first chunk of data being used as a preamble to make sure that the read/write head knows how fast the disk is spinning and therefore how often to sample the magnetic signal.
The next chunk of data is the address of the specific track and sector, which is 48-bits long. Technically that means there are 281 trillion unique addresses which is far more than we need for the current capacities of these drives. After the address, we have the data payload which is around 4KB and after that we have some
Error Correction Code (ECC)
9
bits that allow the drive to know if the data has been read correctly.
The read and write head are actually separate mechanisms. The write head is a tiny coil of copper wire wrapped around a magnetic core - when we write to the disk a current is sent through the copper wire creating a concentrated magnetic field at the tip of the head. The magnetic surface of the disk isn't actually uniform but rather consists of minuscule magnetic grains arranged so that their magnetic fields point perpendicular to the surface.
As the disk spins, the write head very precisely controls its magnetic field to alter the polarity of the magnetic grains, essentially flipping them. If the current flows forward, the magnetic field forces the north pole of the grains to point down and if the current flows in the opposite direction it forces the north pole to face up.
It's tempting to think that we can assign a 0 or a 1 to each grain based on its polarity but because of the way the read head works we can't do this. When two grains with opposite polarities are next to each other they create a much stronger magnetic field and the read head is designed to detect these fields.
The read head is a sandwich of magnetic and non-magnetic fields that change their electrical resistance in the presence of a magnetic field. As the head spins over the disk it reports changes in resistance as a signal, almost like a sound wave, with the largest spikes occurring when there is a change in polarity between neighboring grains.
The way we encode data into the disk is by assigning a 1 to a change in polarity and assigning a 0 to the absence of a change. If we have a string of 0s, or a period with no change in resistance, it can be difficult to know exactly how many bits there are. This is why the preamble is so important, so we can synchronize the bit-rate of the read head with the speed of the disk and work out how many 0s we have.
HDDs have comparatively slow read/write times, so just like with the SSD, they have onboard DRAM so they can read data into a buffer making subsequent reads much faster. The main bottleneck for an HDD is the amount of time it takes to move the arm to a new location so ideally data is co-located as much as possible. This is what defragmenting is about - over time deleted data can leave empty sections making the head travel further for no reason. Defragmenting moves the data around so there are as few gaps as possible.
Unlike Flash SSDs, hard disk drives don't have a write endurance limit but are rather limited by mechanical wear in the actuator and spindle bearings. Once we write to a HDD it can hold that data in the magnetic layer for decades making them one of the best choices for critical data backups.
╌╌╌╌
The holy grail of memory is something that is as fast as SRAM with the density of an SSD and the lifespan of an HDD. Unfortunately for us, we keep running into the pesky laws of physics and so the next best thing is this orchestrated dance of data moving between different levels in the hierarchy as we need it.
Glossary
1
Binary
— A number system using only two digits (0 and 1), which forms the basis of all digital computing.
2
Bit Line
— A vertical conductor in SRAM or DRAM that connects a column of memory cells. It carries the signal to read from or write to the selected cell when the word line for that row is activated.
3
Buffer
— A region of memory used to store data temporarily, often for transferring data between the CPU and GPU or between different stages of a graphics pipeline.
4
Cache
— A small, fast memory located close to the CPU that stores frequently accessed data and instructions to reduce access time.
5
Capacitor
— An electronic component that stores electrical energy in an electric field, used in DRAM to hold the charge representing a single bit of data.
6
CPU
— Central Processing Unit - the main processor in a computer that executes instructions sequentially, optimized for minimizing latency of individual operations.
7
Dielectric
— An insulating material that can be polarized by an electric field, used to separate conductive layers in capacitive touch screens.
8
DRAM (Dynamic RAM)
— Dynamic Random Access Memory - memory that stores each bit in a capacitor, requiring periodic refresh cycles to maintain data but offering higher density than SRAM.
9
Error Correction
— Techniques that detect and correct errors in data transmission or storage by adding redundant information that can be used to verify and reconstruct the original data.
10
GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)
— specialized hardware designed to process many parallel operations simultaneously, particularly for rendering graphics and performing compute-intensive tasks.
11
HDD (Hard Disk Drive)
— A storage device that uses spinning magnetic platters and a moving read/write head to store data, offering high capacity and long-term data retention.
12
Latency
— The time delay between initiating an operation and when it completes, often measured in milliseconds or microseconds.
13
Logic Gate
— A basic building block of digital circuits that performs a Boolean operation (AND, OR, NOT, etc.) on one or more inputs to produce an output.
14
Memory Cell
— The fundamental unit of computer memory that stores a single bit of data, implemented differently in SRAM, DRAM, and flash memory.
15
NAND Flash
— A type of non-volatile memory that stores data in cells arranged in a grid, using charge trap technology to retain data without power.
16
Quantum Tunneling
— A quantum mechanical phenomenon where particles pass through a barrier that would be impossible to cross in classical physics, used in flash memory to move electrons into charge traps.
17
SRAM (Static RAM)
— Static Random Access Memory - fast memory that uses transistor-based flip-flops to store data, retaining it as long as power is supplied without needing refresh cycles.
18
SSD (Solid State Drive)
— A storage device that uses flash memory to store data persistently without moving parts, offering faster access times than traditional hard drives.
19
Transistor
— A semiconductor device used to amplify or switch electronic signals, fundamental to modern electronics and computing.
20
Word Line
— A horizontal control line in SRAM or DRAM that selects an entire row of memory cells. When activated, it opens the access transistors for all cells in that row, connecting them to their bit lines for reading or writing.
╌╌ END ╌╌
Static random access memory
Dynamic random access memory
Solid state drives
Hard disk drives
Glossary

href=https://www.catedraldesal.gov.co/atracciones/espejo-de-agua/ rel>Credit</a><span>.</span></figcaption></figure></div><p><span>In Matthew 5:13–16, Jesus encourages his disciples to be salt in the midst of the world. I’ve always found that image powerful—salt is what gives food its flavor. In family life, in our relationships, in the classroom, in our daily work—in all things—we each have the ability to add that kind of flavor to the moments we share. And we do it in our own way: through our personality, our sense of humor, our presence, and our </span><strong>human values</strong><span>.</span><p><span>In today’s AI-centric world, we may need those “human ingredients” more than ever: joy, humor, deep listening, humility, collaboration, empathy, attention to small details, a word of comfort, the right advice at the right time. </span><strong>These are things AI simply cannot offer</strong><span>. We can sense that AI, for all its power, lacks flavor. Only we can bring depth and richness to </span><a href=https://faculty.washington.edu/ajko/cer#what-is-cer rel>Computing Education</a><span>. Think of the local store customers choose not because they can’t buy the same products online, but because of the warmth of the service, the care, the personal attention—the sense that everything is done with love.</span><p><span>This “salt” is what restores flavor for those who feel </span><a href="https://computingeducationthings.substack.com/p/22-dont-turn-your-brain-off?utm_source=publication-search" rel>disengaged by AI</a><span>, helping preserve integrity not just in </span><a href=https://computingeducationthings.substack.com/p/30-the-fight-to-keep-thinking rel>how we think</a><span>, but also in how we act. Often these values go unnoticed, like a pinch of salt you never see but that transforms the whole dish. The same is true in Computing Education. Our pedagogy should cultivate the human values our moment so desperately needs. But to cultivate them in our students, we must first live them ourselves. If our classes have more flavor because </span><a href="https://computingeducationthings.substack.com/p/7-making-cs-lectures-more-engaging?utm_source=publication-search" rel>they are engaging</a><span>, because we serve with heart, carry a good attitude, and help each student leave with greater clarity than they came with—that alone makes the work worthwhile.</span><p><span>Only a few days remain before the deadline to apply for </span><a href=https://iticse.acm.org/2026/2026-working-group-proposals/#wg10 rel>WG10</a><span> at ITiCSE 2026 (</span><em>Teamwork in Computing Education: Skills, Values, and Virtues</em><span>)— I’ve already applied!</span><div><hr></div><h2 class=header-anchor-post><strong>A Lesser-Known Bottleneck in AI Scalability</strong><div y2=14></line></svg></button></div></div></div></a></figure></div><p>In this week’s Numerical Analysis class, we covered interpolation and fitting, and it turned into a good opportunity to think about a question that keeps coming up in AI conversations: scalability.<p><span>That’s where </span><a href=https://theconversation.com/la-electronica-y-el-limite-fisico-que-ignoramos-cuando-hablamos-de-ia-272634 rel>this article</a><span> by </span><a href=https://www.unir.net/profesores/paula-lamo-anuarbe/ rel>Paula Lamo</a><span>, a former professor of mine from a Computer Technology course, fits in nicely. She explores a lesser-known bottleneck that’s increasingly shaping the limits of AI. It’s not just about how much electricity is consumed, but about a more subtle and deeply technical constraint: </span><a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_electronics rel>power electronics</a><span>. As power density rises in the accelerators used to train and run AI models, managing and converting energy becomes a critical design challenge. Inefficiencies at this level lead to heat, instability, and hard physical limits that software alone can’t overcome.</span><p>Many of the infrastructure and cost issues we see today trace back to this very specific physical constraint. I found this piece especially valuable because it pushes back against the dominant narrative that places most of the emphasis on data and code, and instead highlights how the future of AI is increasingly constrained by physical and engineering realities.<blockquote><p><span>Those who have lived in software land don’t realize they’re about to have a hard lesson in hardware - </span><a href=https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/elon-musk rel>Elon Musk on the Dwarkesh podcast</a><span>.</span></p></blockquote><div><hr></div><h2 class=header-anchor-post><strong>What skills do CS students need?</strong><div class="pencraft pc-display-flex pc-alignItems-center pc-position-absolute pc-reset header-anchor-parent"><div class="pencraft pc-display-contents pc-reset pubTheme-yiXxQA"><div id=§what-skills-do-cs-students-need class="pencraft pc-reset header-anchor offset-top"></div><button type=button aria-label=Link data-href=https://computingeducationthings.substack.com/i/187382023/what-skills-do-cs-students-need class="pencraft pc-reset iconButton-mq_Et5 iconButtonBase-dJGHgN buttonBase-GK1x3M buttonStyle-r7yGCK size_sm-G3LciD priority_secondary-S63h9o" tabindex=0><svg xmlns=http://www.w3.org/2000/svg width=18 height=18 viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill=none stroke=currentColor stroke-width=2 stroke-linecap=round stroke-linejoin=round class="lucide lucide-link"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></button></div></div></h2><p>In the new job market shaped by AI, technical fluency alone is no longer enough. We need to think of AI not just as a tool, but as an “e-bike for the mind”—something that can extend our range, but also magnify our mistakes. In my opinion, it is important for CS students to develop four key skills:<ol><li><p><strong>Technical fluency:</strong><span> knowing how to use AI tools effectively, but also understanding how they work (and how they fail).</span></p><li><p><strong>Ethical reasoning:</strong><span> the ability to wrestle with real trade-offs and to think seriously about societal, environmental, and human consequences.</span></p><li><p><strong>Creative agency</strong><span>: using AI to expand human capability rather than outsourcing thinking to it—maintaining ownership over ideas, design, and direction.</span></p><li><p><strong>Critical judgment</strong><span>: knowing when to trust, verify, or reject AI outputs, and even when not to build something at all.</span></p></ol><p>If we want to prepare the next generation of computer scientists thoughtfully, CS educators should make space to intentionally teach and model these four capacities—not just as complementary topics, but as important parts of a well-rounded formation.<div class=captioned-image-container><figure><a target=_blank  </span><path classname=inner-triangle d="M10 8L16 12L10 16V8Z" stroke-width=1.5 stroke-linecap=round stroke-linejoin=round></path><span>
</span></div><span class=embedded-post-cta>Listen now</span></div><div class=embedded-post-meta>4 days ago · 21 likes · 1 comment · Ryan Peterman</div></a></div><p><a href=https://www.linkedin.com/in/adamjernst/ rel>Adam Ernst</a><span> graduated in Computer Science from Princeton in 2010 and joined Meta in 2012, just ahead of the company’s IPO, during the mobile rewrite era. He has since spent more than 13 years at Meta, where he is now a Distinguished Engineer (IC9), building and leading critical iOS infrastructure with company-wide impact. In this conversation, Adam walks through his career—from early projects to ambitious platform bets—sharing concrete lessons on growing as an individual contributor, influencing without authority, and learning from both success and failure.</span><h3 class=header-anchor-post><strong>Early Builder Mindset</strong><div class="pencraft pc-display-flex pc-alignItems-center pc-position-absolute pc-reset header-anchor-parent"><div class="pencraft pc-display-contents pc-reset pubTheme-yiXxQA"><div id=§early-builder-mindset class="pencraft pc-reset header-anchor offset-top"></div><button type=button aria-label=Link data-href=https://computingeducationthings.substack.com/i/187382023/early-builder-mindset class="pencraft pc-reset iconButton-mq_Et5 iconButtonBase-dJGHgN buttonBase-GK1x3M buttonStyle-r7yGCK size_sm-G3LciD priority_secondary-S63h9o" tabindex=0><svg xmlns=http://www.w3.org/2000/svg width=18 height=18 viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill=none stroke=currentColor stroke-width=2 stroke-linecap=round stroke-linejoin=round class="lucide lucide-link"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></button></div></div></h3><p><span>Adam’s trajectory starts long before Meta: as a middle-schooler he built and sold a real product (“Cosmic Soft”)—online testing software for teachers—using a beginner-friendly tool (RealBasic). He even handled payments through a proto-Stripe service (eSellerate) and accepted checks by mail, emailing license codes back. My takeaway: </span><strong>build something useful, get it into the world, learn by shipping</strong><span>.</span><h3 class=header-anchor-post><strong>Scaling iOS at Facebook</strong><div class="pencraft pc-display-flex pc-alignItems-center pc-position-absolute pc-reset header-anchor-parent"><div class="pencraft pc-display-contents pc-reset pubTheme-yiXxQA"><div id=§scaling-ios-at-facebook class="pencraft pc-reset header-anchor offset-top"></div><button type=button aria-label=Link data-href=https://computingeducationthings.substack.com/i/187382023/scaling-ios-at-facebook class="pencraft pc-reset iconButton-mq_Et5 iconButtonBase-dJGHgN buttonBase-GK1x3M buttonStyle-r7yGCK size_sm-G3LciD priority_secondary-S63h9o" tabindex=0><svg xmlns=http://www.w3.org/2000/svg width=18 height=18 viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill=none stroke=currentColor stroke-width=2 stroke-linecap=round stroke-linejoin=round class="lucide lucide-link"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></button></div></div></h3><p>He joined Facebook in 2012 (right before the IPO) during the shift from an HTML5 app to a native rewrite—an environment where scaling problems created unusually large opportunities. His early impact came from replacing Apple’s CoreData, which didn’t scale to a rapidly growing iOS org. The key lesson: architect for scale while enabling incremental adoption (e.g., immutable “memmodels” to reason about thread safety and change safely across a fast-moving codebase).<h3 class=header-anchor-post><strong>Influence without authority</strong><div class="pencraft pc-display-flex pc-alignItems-center pc-position-absolute pc-reset header-anchor-parent"><div class="pencraft pc-display-contents pc-reset pubTheme-yiXxQA"><div id=§influence-without-authority class="pencraft pc-reset header-anchor offset-top"></div><button type=button aria-label=Link data-href=https://computingeducationthings.substack.com/i/187382023/influence-without-authority class="pencraft pc-reset iconButton-mq_Et5 iconButtonBase-dJGHgN buttonBase-GK1x3M buttonStyle-r7yGCK size_sm-G3LciD priority_secondary-S63h9o" tabindex=0><svg xmlns=http://www.w3.org/2000/svg width=18 height=18 viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill=none stroke=currentColor stroke-width=2 stroke-linecap=round stroke-linejoin=round class="lucide lucide-link"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></button></div></div></h3><p><span>A recurring theme is how Adam persuades other software engineers without formal power: talk live when possible, acknowledge the other side’s worldview (“I like vanilla Apple frameworks too”), and arrive with data (even reverse-engineering black-box behavior when needed). His most effective tactic: </span><strong>do the work for people</strong><span>—show up with a migration or fix already implemented so the task becomes “approve” rather than “take on a huge task.” He applies that same influence model through code review, treating it as a concrete forum for technical dialogue—using real diffs to explain trade-offs, surface assumptions, and shape how other software engineers reason about code.</span><h3 class=header-anchor-post><strong>High-stakes platform bets</strong><div class="pencraft pc-display-flex pc-alignItems-center pc-position-absolute pc-reset header-anchor-parent"><div class="pencraft pc-display-contents pc-reset pubTheme-yiXxQA"><div id=§high-stakes-platform-bets class="pencraft pc-reset header-anchor offset-top"></div><button type=button aria-label=Link data-href=https://computingeducationthings.substack.com/i/187382023/high-stakes-platform-bets class="pencraft pc-reset iconButton-mq_Et5 iconButtonBase-dJGHgN buttonBase-GK1x3M buttonStyle-r7yGCK size_sm-G3LciD priority_secondary-S63h9o" tabindex=0><svg xmlns=http://www.w3.org/2000/svg width=18 height=18 viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill=none stroke=currentColor stroke-width=2 stroke-linecap=round stroke-linejoin=round class="lucide lucide-link"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></button></div></div></h3><p>Adam’s senior-career arc is shaped by high-risk, platform-level bets. With ComponentKit, he helped introduce React-inspired declarative UI ideas to iOS years before SwiftUI or React Native, addressing News Feed complexity through components, immutability, and better performance—while navigating significant internal skepticism and the need for sustained buy-in across teams. The counterweight was ComponentScript, a cross-platform framework that was technically sound but failed to gain traction. Adam is explicit about why: unclear target users, real adoption friction, and ecosystem dynamics mattered as much as the quality of the architecture itself. His takeaway is clear and hard-earned: strong technical ideas still fail without alignment, incentives, and momentum—and senior engineers must be willing to shut projects down responsibly when they don’t work.<h3 class=header-anchor-post><strong>Technical Depth</strong><div class="pencraft pc-display-flex pc-alignItems-center pc-position-absolute pc-reset header-anchor-parent"><div class="pencraft pc-display-contents pc-reset pubTheme-yiXxQA"><div id=§technical-depth class="pencraft pc-reset header-anchor offset-top"></div><button type=button aria-label=Link data-href=https://computingeducationthings.substack.com/i/187382023/technical-depth class="pencraft pc-reset iconButton-mq_Et5 iconButtonBase-dJGHgN buttonBase-GK1x3M buttonStyle-r7yGCK size_sm-G3LciD priority_secondary-S63h9o" tabindex=0><svg xmlns=http://www.w3.org/2000/svg width=18 height=18 viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill=none stroke=currentColor stroke-width=2 stroke-linecap=round stroke-linejoin=round class="lucide lucide-link"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></button></div></div></h3><p>Rather than chasing trends or frequently switching domains, Adam deliberately stayed deep in mobile infrastructure, allowing real problems to pull him into adjacent systems when needed. When blocked by GraphQL, build tooling, or codegen, he didn’t escalate—he dove in, traced the issue several layers deep, and either fixed it himself or arrived with a precise diagnosis. Over time, this pattern compounded into broad system knowledge rooted in necessity. Combined with his bias toward writing and reviewing real code, that depth became his leverage as an IC: influence earned through proximity to the work, not through titles or constant reinvention.<div><hr></div><h3 class=header-anchor-post><strong>→ Bots, Agents, and Leverage</strong><div class="pencraft pc-display-flex pc-alignItems-center pc-position-absolute pc-reset header-anchor-parent"><div class="pencraft pc-display-contents pc-reset pubTheme-yiXxQA"><div id=§bots-agents-and-leverage class="pencraft pc-reset header-anchor offset-top"></div><button type=button aria-label=Link data-href=https://computingeducationthings.substack.com/i/187382023/bots-agents-and-leverage class="pencraft pc-reset iconButton-mq_Et5 iconButtonBase-dJGHgN buttonBase-GK1x3M buttonStyle-r7yGCK size_sm-G3LciD priority_secondary-S63h9o" tabindex=0><svg xmlns=http://www.w3.org/2000/svg width=18 height=18 viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill=none stroke=currentColor stroke-width=2 stroke-linecap=round stroke-linejoin=round class="lucide lucide-link"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></button></div></div></h3><div id=youtube2-hU83uz1h0z4 data-attrs='{"videoId":"hU83uz1h0z4","startTime":null,"endTime":null}' data-component-name=Youtube2ToDOM class=youtube-wrap><div class=youtube-inner></div></div><p><span>In this conversation with Aman Manazir, </span><a href=https://www.linkedin.com/in/ritesh-verma-techpreneur/ rel>Ritesh Verma</a><span> explains how he went from a traditional computer science path (University of Maryland, internship and full-time offer at Capital One) to making more from side hustles than from his six-figure software engineering job. His journey started with experimentation: a viral SAT YouTube channel in college, then niche automation projects like checkout bots that attracted high-paying clients.</span><p>Over time, he realized that what people now call “AI agents” are often just automation software with an AI layer—the evolution of the same bots he had been building for years. To him, the technical barrier is lower than people think. Tools like no-code automation platforms, web automation libraries, and AI-assisted coding environments mean that most software engineers already have more than enough skill to compete.<blockquote><p>Computer science students are the best people to do this because of their unique advantage over anyone else.</p></blockquote><p>The real differentiator is identifying a clear problem, packaging a solution quickly, and getting it in front of buyers. He repeatedly emphasizes that many profitable agents are simple: AI chatbots trained on a company’s website to capture leads instantly, automated content systems for e-commerce brands, or niche workflows that save small businesses hours of manual work. His playbook is deliberately practical: start with a niche you can access, find a time-consuming process, build a live demo, price it low enough to remove friction for the first customer, capture a video testimonial, and turn that into a landing page. He stresses that credibility compounds: once you have one paying client and proof of results, the second and third come much faster. Instead of building a perfect product in isolation, he advocates building in public and using real-world case studies as marketing fuel.<p>Distribution, in his view, is the true moat. Short-form content can generate attention quickly. X (Twitter) allows builders to tap into “build in public” communities. But he highlights Reddit as especially powerful: transparent posts about revenue milestones or lessons learned—without links, calls-to-action, or overt selling—can drive serious inbound leads. If the story is compelling enough, prospects will find a way to reach out.<p>Underneath the tactics is a broader philosophy. Ritesh sees this path not as hype, but as economic self-defense in a market defined by layoffs, shrinking junior roles, and increasing automation inside large companies. In his view, software engineers should treat side hustles not as hobbies but as leverage—cash-flowing systems that reduce dependence on a single employer. And if someone chooses to leave a salaried role, he suggests a simple rule: don’t quit for the dream—quit when the business reliably earns two to three times your salary.<div href=https://www.afueradentro.com/ rel>afueradentro</a></em><span> ties into what I talked about in </span><a href=https://computingeducationthings.substack.com/p/31-the-confidence-trap-the-illusion rel>last week’s newsletter</a><span>—about drawing from other disciplines so we don’t end up living in a bubble: Having a hobby changes your Instagram algorithm, so you’re not constantly seeing the same stuff. For anyone working in the cultural or creative industries, it’s important to be immersed in different things.</span><p><a href="https://x.com/bcherny/status/2017742741636321619/?rw_tt_thread=True" rel>Interesting thread</a><span> by Boris Cherny with some tips on how to get the most out of Claude Code. Along those lines, I loved </span><a href=https://mitchellh.com/writing/my-ai-adoption-journey rel>this article</a><span> by </span><a href=https://mitchellh.com/ rel>Mitchell Hashimoto</a><span> about his journey adopting AI into his workflow.</span><p><span>Heard </span><a href="https://youtu.be/biLg6fljDLo?si=If5Uc-06enEta2LX" rel>here</a><span>: </span><em>Andrej Karpathy is a great professor — it’s hard to find someone so technical who can explain things so clearly.</em><p><span>A highlight from ACM’s interview with </span><a href=https://www.linkedin.com/in/pei-cao-01940317/ rel>Pei Cao</a><span>, VP of Engineering at YouTube: Computer science is a fast-changing field. Every decade brings new challenges that require communities of researchers to solve. As you advance in your career, you won’t always work in the technical subareas in which you were trained. </span><a href="https://computingeducationthings.substack.com/p/10-focusing-on-the-cs-fundamentals?utm_source=publication-search" rel>But a solid computer science foundation will enable you to learn any subfield of computer science quickly</a><span> and then make contributions. So be prepared to </span><a href="https://computingeducationthings.substack.com/p/23-what-it-means-to-be-a-software?utm_source=publication-search" rel>learn continuously</a><span> and don’t be afraid to venture into new areas.</span><p><a href=https://www.linkedin.com/in/brendangregg/ rel>Brendan Gregg</a><span> is joining OpenAI. What a gig! There are very few places right now where the link between system performance and real business value is as strong as it is there.</span><p>I loved this piece from Julian Lehr, Creative Director at Linear, laying out a thoughtful case against conversational interfaces.<div data-attrs='{"id":160019274,"url":"https://julianlehr.substack.com/p/the-case-against-conversational-interfaces","publication_id":53774,"publication_name":"julian.digital","publication_logo_url":"https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!u_ao!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa2a07d70-3d4b-48fa-80be-d563fcdf8ba6_1280x1280.png","title":"The case against conversational interfaces","truncated_body_text":"Intro Conversational interfaces are a bit of a meme. It looks like they’re trying to stand out from the competition by giving users the option to have a more controlled experience—based on their own preferences.</span><p><span>Thought-provoking piece from Josh Brake on what </span><a href=https://blog.cosmos-institute.org/p/the-philosopher-builder rel>Cosmos</a><span> calls the philosopher-builder.</span><blockquote><p>At Mudd, the humanities, social sciences, and the arts are integrated throughout the curriculum. Breadth is a feature, not a bug.<p>If the first duty of the educator is formational, the question we need to ask is not “what are they learning?” but “who are they becoming?” What habits and practices are we helping our students to cultivate? What questions are we teaching them to ask?</p></blockquote><div data-attrs='{"id":187594840,"url":"https://joshbrake.substack.com/p/cultivating-philosopher-builders","publication_id":634571,"publication_name":"The Absent-Minded Professor","publication_logo_url":"https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dJt2!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe88f1d7a-77bc-453c-aa04-2ef949a57f80_1280x1280.png","title":"Cultivating Philosopher-Builders","truncated_body_text":"Thank you for being here. And I’ve been saying this for a while saying, Oh, and by the way, the most powerful technology that we just invented, the internet, we’re going to weaponize and we’re going to abuse it. It’s going to be abused powerfully. And this is the thing, </span><strong>the more powerful the technology, the more powerfully it will be abused</strong><span>. That’s the nature of it. AI, man, it will be really abused. However, and this is the curious thing, even those abuses of technology are increased choices. When the first humanoid picked up a rock and turns it into a hammer, either to make a shelter or to kill his brother, he suddenly had a new choice he never had before. </span><strong>That choice is good</strong><span>.</span><p><a href=https://every.to/source-code/compound-engineering-how-every-codes-with-agents-af3a1bae-cf9b-458e-8048-c6b4ba860e62 rel>This piece</a><span> from Every introduces </span><strong>compound engineering</strong><span>, a model where AI writes the code and software engineering centers on a four-step loop: plan, work, assess, and compound. UH. One of them presented by </span><a href=https://www.linkedin.com/in/gen-li-b6958b192/ rel>Gen Li</a><span>, a third-year Ph.D. student at Clemson University, where he focused on the evolution of modern AI models and the growing challenges related to efficiency, safety, and real-world deployment and where he shared concrete research on dynamic sparse training, selective unlearning, and adversarial defenses—techniques that help make large models more practical, robust, and trustworthy under real-world constraints. The second seminar, given by </span><a href=https://northwestern.jerryhu.page/ rel>Jerry Yao-Chieh Hu</a><span> from Northwestern, took a more theoretical turn, offering a unifying view of what transformers actually do. He framed transformers around two core capabilities—memory and procedure execution—showing how attention can be interpreted as a physical memory retrieval process and how a single fixed model can act as a universal program executor when prompts are treated as programs. The talk connected deep theory with large-scale scientific applications in genomics and astrophysics, shedding light on why foundation models generalize so effectively across tasks.</span><p>I learned a lot from these two potential UH tenure-track faculty members.</p></blockquote><blockquote><p>Next week, from February 18 to 21, I’ll be attending the SIGCSE TS 2026 conference in St. Louis, Missouri. You don’t “solve” a marriage once and for all—“I’ll never solve my marriage. I can only live in my marriage.” In the same way, you don’t solve CS and move on; you live in it, wrestle with it, grow through it. The confusion, the bugs, the conceptual friction—those aren’t obstacles to learning. They are THE learning. In complex domains, you cannot skip the difficulty.</span><p><span>I highly recommend the BBC podcast </span><em><a href=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b006qnmr rel>Desert Island Discs</a></em><span>, where each guest is asked to imagine they’re stranded on a deserted island. They have to choose eight albums, one book, and one personal item. Through their choices, you get a deep, revealing portrait of the castaway featured in each episode. TITLE: Persistent {{Anti-Muslim Bias}} in {{Large Language Models}}
AUTHOR: Abid, Abubakar and Farooqi, Maheen and Zou, James
YEAR: 2021
THEMES: Data & Platform Ecosystems
ABSTRACT: Demonstrates that GPT-3 consistently associates Muslim identity with violence across multiple prompting contexts, revealing how training data encodes and amplifies religious bias at scale.
WHY INCLUDED: Provides a concrete, testable case of bias embedded in large language models, grounding abstract discussions of algorithmic discrimination in measurable outcomes students can examine critically.

--- Page 1 ---
Persistent Anti-Muslim Bias in Large Language Models
Abubakar Abid1, Maheen Farooqi2, James Zou3∗
1DepartmentofElectricalEngineering,StanfordUniversity,CA,USA
2DepartmentofHealthSciences,McMasterUniversity,ON,Canada
3DepartmentofBiomedicalDataScience,StanfordUniversity,CA,USA
∗Towhomcorrespondenceshouldbeaddressed: jamesz@stanford.edu.
Ithasbeenobservedthatlarge-scalelanguagemodelscaptureundesirableso-
cietal biases, e.g. relating to race and gender; yet religious bias has been rel-
atively unexplored. We demonstrate that GPT-3, a state-of-the-art contextual
language model, captures persistent Muslim-violence bias. We probe GPT-3
invariousways,includingpromptcompletion,analogicalreasoning,andstory
generation,tounderstandthisanti-Muslimbias,demonstratingthatitappears
consistently and creatively in different uses of the model and that it is severe
evencomparedtobiasesaboutotherreligiousgroups. Forinstance,“Muslim”
is analogized to “terrorist” in 23% of test cases, while “Jewish” is mapped to
“money” in 5% of test cases. We quantify the positive distraction needed to
overcomethisbiaswithadversarialtextprompts,andfindthatuseofthemost
positive 6 adjectives reduces violent completions for “Muslims” from 66% to
20%,butwhichisstillhigherthanforotherreligiousgroups.
In recent years, natural language processing (NLP) research has seen substantial progress
onavarietyoftasksbypretraininglanguagemodelsonlargecorporaoftextinanunsupervised

manner. These language models have evolved, from learning individual word vectors with
single-layer models (1), to more complex language generation architectures such as recurrent
neural networks (2) and most recently transformers (3–5). As more complex language models
havebeendeveloped,theneedforfine-tuningthemwithtask-specificdatasetsandtask-specific
architectures has also become less important, with the most recent transformer-based architec-
tures requiring very few, if any, task-specific examples to do well in a particular NLP task. As
a result, methods research is increasingly focused on better language models and, we show in
thispaper,soshouldthescrutinyforlearnedbiasesandundesiredlinguisticassociations.
Trainingalanguagemodelrequiresalargecorpusofpre-writtentext. Thelanguagemodelis
providedrandomsnippetsoftextfromthecorpusandistaskedwithpredictingthenextwordof
thesnippet,giventhepreviouswordsasthecontext1. Todowellonthistaskrequiresthemodel
tolearncorrectsyntax,aswellaslearntypicalassociationsbetweenwords,sothatitcanpredict
the most likely word to follow. What associations does the model learn for any given word? It
is clear that this depends on how the word was used in the corpus itself. Most researchers do
not extensively curate the corpus to shape the associations learned by the model; in fact, such
an approach is infeasible given the scale of these datasets2. Instead, raw text from websites
scraped across the internet is generally used to feed the model, with little considerations of the
biases that may be present in the data3. As a result, even though the various language models
have different architectures, since they are trained on similar corpora of text, they often learn
similarbiases(6).
Previousworkhasexploredthebiasesthatareultimatelylearnedbylanguagemodels,with
the primary focus being racial and gender stereotypes (7–10). For example, in (7), the authors
noted that word embeddings could be probed through analogies to identify sexist biases that

Inthispaper,wefurtherinvestigateanti-Muslimbiasinlanguagemodels,quantifyingitand
noting its prevalence across different tasks. We focus on GPT-3 (4), not only as it is the largest
existing language model, but also because it has captured particularly powerful linguistic asso-
ciations,allowingittoperformwelleveninthefew-shotsettingwithoutfurtherfine-tuning. For
example, GPT-3 answers multiple-choice analogies in the form of “audaciousness is to bold-
ness as: (a) sanctimonious is to hypocrisy, (b) anonymous is to identity, (c) ...” correctly 55%
of the time, in the zero-shot setting. When provided with a single correctly-answered example,
that accuracy increases to 59%, better than the average college student, who correctly answers
suchquestions57%ofthetime(4,11). Becauseofitsimpressiveperformanceonvariousnatu-
rallanguagetasks,particularlyanalogies,whichrequirelearningcomplexassociationsbetween
words, we focus on GPT-3 in this report and investigate the associations that the model has
learnedabouttheword“Muslim.”
Tocarryoutthisinvestigation,weutilizebothaprogrammaticAPIthatOpenAIcreatedfor
GPT-3, as well as the OpenAI’s GPT-3 Playground. Both were released to select researchers
and developers to run predictions with the model. The Playground and the API allow users to
provide an initial prompt and then run a command to generate the subsequent words (or com-
pletion) according to the learned language model. A depiction of the graphical user interface
fortheOpenAIPlaygroundisshowninFig. 1(a).

Results
Toinvestigateanti-Muslimbias,wefirstexaminetheoutputofGPT-3whentheword“Muslim”
is included in the prompt. As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), we observe that the resulting completion
can include violent language. To quantify the magnitude of this bias, we fix the prompt to be
a neutral phrase: “Two Muslims walked into a”, and run GPT-3 100 times4 to observe 100
different completions. A representative set of 5 completions is shown in Fig. 1(b). We observe
that 66 out of the 100 completions are violent, by which we mean that the completion contains
violence-related words/phrases such as shooting, killing, etc. (see Supplementary Materials
for full list of keywords). Replacing “Muslims” with terms for other religious groups, we
find that violent completions are significantly less likely for other religious groups (Fig. 1(c)).
By examining the completions, we see that GPT-3 does not memorize a small set of violent
headlines about Muslims; rather, it manifests its Muslim-violence association in creative ways
byvaryingtheweapons,nature,andsettingoftheviolenceinvolved.
Previous analyses of language models have demonstrated that biases can be revealed by
looking at the embeddings of words and phrases and forming analogies in the embedding
space (7). Although we do not have access to GPT-3’s learned embeddings, we can probe
the associations that GPT-3 has learned for different religious groups by asking it to directly
answer open-ended analogies. We used a similar setup to the original work (4), in which we
present GPT-3 with the following analogy: “audacious is to boldness as Muslim is to...” and
askGPT-3tocompletetheanalogyinazero-shotsetting. BypresentingGPT-3withananalogy
consistingofanadjectiveandsimilarnoun,andreplacing“Muslim”withotherreligiousadjec-
tives, we can directly assess the model’s closely-associated nouns with each of these religious
terms.

Finally, we demonstrate bias in long-form completions, by using GPT-3 to generate long
descriptivecaptionsfromphotos5. Thesedescriptionsaregeneratedbypassingimagesthrough
apretrainedimagecaptioningmodel(12),andfine-tuningGPT-3totransformtheshortcaptions
intolongdescriptions,asshowninFig. 3(a)-(b). WecreatedavisualinterfaceusingtheGradio
library (13), and used the model to generate captions for stock photos. We find that typical
descriptions are humorous or poignant, reflecting the examples that are provided to GPT-3 in
the context (see Fig. 3(c) and Supplementary Materials). However, the descriptions generated
by GPT-3 are violent when it is fed short captions that include Muslim religious attire, such as
headscarf. WeshowonesuchexampleinFig. 3(d),seealsoSupplementaryMaterials.
When the word “Muslim” is included in the prompt, it is difficult to generate GPT-3 com-
pletions that do not contain violent language. For example, even when the prompt is modi-
fied to read “Two Muslims walked into a mosque to worship peacefully,” the completions are
consistently violent. In our experiments, we found that the most reliable way to debias6 the
completionswasbyintroducingashortphraseintothepromptthatcarriedpositiveassociations
about Muslims. This is inspired by “adversarial triggers” (14), which are short sequences of
wordsthatchangelanguagemodelsoutputs. Forexample,modifyingtheprompttoread“Mus-
lims are hard-working. Two Muslims walked into a” produced non-violent completions about
80% of the time. Fig. 4(a) illustrates this debiasing strategy. Listed in Fig. 4(b) are the 50
positive adjectives that we tried, which are randomly selected from a precompiled list7 of such
words. We fed 500 such prompts including positive triggers with all 50 adjectives into GPT-3
and found that averaged across all results, the proportion of violence-containing completions
dropped from 66% to 46%. We then repeated this experiment with 120 prompts using only the
6 best-performing adjectives, and found that we could further reduce the violent completions

Discussion
Our investigation demonstrates that GPT-3, a powerful language model, captures strong neg-
ative stereotypes regarding the word “Muslim” that appear in different uses of the language
model. While these associations between Muslims and violence are learned during pretrain-
ing, they do not seem to be memorized; rather, GPT-3 manifests the underlying biases quite
creatively, demonstrating the powerful ability of language models to mutate biases in different
ways,whichmaymakethebiasesmoredifficulttodetectandmitigate.
Ourexperimentsalsodemonstratethatitispossibletoreducethebiasinthecompletionsof
GPT-3toacertainextentbyintroducingwordsandphrasesintothecontextthatprovidestrong
positiveassociations. Inourexperiments,wehavecarriedouttheseinterventionsmanually,and
found that a side effect of introducing these words was to redirect the focus of language model
towardsaveryspecifictopic,andthusitmaynotbeageneralsolution. Itremainstobestudied
whetherthisprocesscanbeautomatedandoptimized.
